items.title: The most iconic food in every state
items.summary: From Maine's famous lobster rolls to Tennessee's Nashville hot chicken, every state is known for an iconic dish. Rabbitti/Getty Images Every state has an iconic dish, whether it was invented or popularized there, or drives the local economy. Maine and Connecticut are both famous for their lobster rolls , though they prepare them differently. Other states have famous sandwiches, stews, or dips. From seafood staples and regional sandwiches to hearty stews and decadent desserts, every state has a dish that reflects its history, culture, and local ingredients. We identified each state's most iconic food based on its regional or national recognition, historical or cultural ties to the state, and its enduring place in the state's culinary identity. Several have become nationally famous, including Illinois' deep-dish pizza and Tennessee's Nashville hot chicken, served by restaurants such as Hattie B's . Others are beloved regional specialties, including Maine's famous cold lobster rolls with mayonnaise and Colorado's over-the-top Fool's Gold sandwich. Some are also tied to major industries that support jobs, tourism, and local economies within their states, such as Alaska's salmon , Wisconsin's cheese, and Virginia's oysters. Here's the most iconic local dish from every state. ALABAMA: Chicken with white barbecue sauce Chicken with white barbecue sauce. Jacek Chabraszewski/Shutterstock Alabama's famous white barbecue sauce, which is made with mayonnaise, vinegar, salt, and ground black pepper, is described as both creamy and tangy. The sauce, which is said to have been invented in the 1920s by Bob Gibson of Big Bob Gibson Bar-B-Q in Decatur, Alabama, often comes served on a sandwich or with grilled or fried chicken. ALASKA: Smoked salmon Smoked salmon. Frank Perry/AFP via Getty Images Alaska is famous for its salmon, though locals may disagree on the best way to prepare it — whether that's smoked, grilled, or pan-seared. For a classic Alaskan meal, serve the fish with seasonal vegetables, or enjoy smoked salmon on a bagel with cream cheese. ARIZONA: Chimichangas Chimichangas. Ezume Images/Shutterstock You might not know that chimichangas were invented in Arizona. As Tucson Foodie reported, two restaurants in Tucson claim to have originated the dish, a large meat burrito filled with vegetables and spices, deep-fried, and topped with cheese and sauce. ARKANSAS: Fried pickles Fried pickles. Kay Ecker/Shutterstock Fans of fried pickles have Arkansas to thank for the iconic snack. The first fried dill pickles ever sold anywhere first appeared on the menu of the Duchess Drive-In in Atkins, Arkansas, in the summer of 1963, Encyclopedia of Arkansas reported. CALIFORNIA: Avocado toast Avocado toast. Alexander Spatari/Getty Images California is famous for its avocados, so it should come as no surprise that avocado toast is one of the most popular and famous local dishes in the Golden State. The San Francisco Chronicle reported that California residents have been making avocado toast for more than 130 years. An issue of The Daily Alta California from 1885 lists a recipe that suggests spreading avocado "on slices of bread, and season with salt and pepper." COLORADO: The "Fool's Gold" sandwich "Fool's Gold" sandwiches. Karl Gehring/The Denver Post/Getty Images The now-closed Colorado Mine Company restaurant in Denver invented the original Fool's Gold sandwich: a hollowed-out loaf of sourdough stuffed with peanut butter, blueberry jam, and a pound of bacon. The over-the-top sandwich became legendary after Elvis Presley reportedly loved it so much that he flew his private jet to Denver and back in a single night just to eat one. CONNECTICUT: Warm lobster rolls Lobster roll. Rebecca Fondren Photo/Shutterstock Culture Trip reported that the first documented lobster roll was served at a Milford, Connecticut, restaurant named Perry's in 1929. Although you may be more familiar with Maine-style lobster rolls served cold with mayonnaise, Connecticut has its own signature take. A traditional Connecticut-style lobster roll features warm lobster meat lightly dressed with melted butter and served on a split-top bun. DELAWARE: Peach pie Peach pie. zoryanchik/Shutterstock Delaware's official state dessert is peach pie, and peaches are an integral part of the state's agricultural industry. According to the Delaware government, peaches have been an important part of the state's agricultural heritage since their introduction during Colonial times, when they became a major industry in the 19th century. At the industry's peak in 1875, Delaware shipped about 6 million baskets of peaches to market. FLORIDA: Cuban sandwiches Cuban Sandwich. Old Republic Kitchen and Bar/Yelp While these sandwiches can, of course, be traced back to Cuba, what we know now as a "Cuban sandwich" is largely thanks to Cuban immigrants in Tampa, Florida. Thrillist reported that the sandwiches made in Cuba and the United States had a few key differences when it came to ingredients. The Florida version, which sometimes used imported Italian salami, became known as a "Cuban sandwich." GEORGIA: Brunswick stew Brunswick stew. ButtermilkgirlVirginia/Shutterstock Both Brunswick County, Virginia, and Brunswick, Georgia, claim to be the birthplace of Brunswick stew. In Brunswick, Georgia, a town monument features a 25-gallon iron pot with an inscription stating that the first batch of Brunswick stew was cooked in it in 1898. HAWAII: Kālua pork Kalua pork nachos. Maricay/Shutterstock Kālua pork is one of Hawaii's most iconic dishes. The smoked, shredded pork — sometimes mixed with cabbage — is traditionally cooked in an underground oven, which is reflected in its name: "kālua" means "to cook in an underground oven" in Hawaiian. IDAHO: Finger steaks Finger steaks. Paul_Brighton/Shutterstock Many have traced the origin of finger steaks — fried pieces of beef — back to Milo's Torch Lounge in Boise. Idaho Beef says chef Milo Bybee invented the dish in 1957 to use the restaurant's leftover tenderloin. ILLINOIS: Deep-dish pizza Giordano's. Irene Jiang/Business Insider While you might assume that all pizza originates in Italy, deep-dish pizza is actually American. The BBC reported that restaurant owners Ike Sewell and Ric Riccardo introduced their creation, an Italian-American pizza they called deep-dish, at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago's Near North Side neighborhood in 1943. INDIANA: Pork tenderloin sandwiches A Hoosier sandwich. Jeff R Clow/Getty Images Pork tenderloin sandwiches, also called "Hoosier sandwiches," can be traced back to Nick Freienstein, a Huntington, Indiana, native-born to German parents. Eater reported the dish was originally inspired by Wiener schnitzel, a Viennese-style veal dish that is breaded and pan-fried. In 1904, Freienstein began selling sandwiches and burgers out of a food cart. While veal was hard to come by in his hometown, pork was readily available. After he added pickles and onions to his fried pork tenderloin sandwich, Freienstein's cart took off. He is credited with creating the first "Hoosier sandwich." IOWA: Fried catfish Fried catfish and fries. HMR2017/Shutterstock While fried catfish is a popular dish throughout the South, Iowans are fond of it as well. KANSAS: Loose meat sandwiches Loose meat sandwiches. P Lansing/Shutterstock A cross between a sloppy Joe and a cheeseburger, loose meat sandwiches are a favorite among Kansas locals. The Nu-Way Cafe, a Wichita-based chain of restaurants, is famous for its loose meat sandwiches. In other parts of the country, they are known as tavern sandwiches or Maid-Rites, named after the Iowa chain. KENTUCKY: Beer cheese Beer cheese. Africa Studio/Shutterstock According to local lore, beer cheese was invented by Chef Joe Allman for his cousin Johnnie, the owner of the Driftwood Inn near Winchester, Kentucky. The Downtown Winchester Beer Cheese Festival reported that the dish was originally created by Allman to entice customers to order more beer with their meals. LOUISIANA: Gumbo Chicken and sausage gumbo. Ken Durden/Shutterstock Gumbo, a traditional stew consisting primarily of a strong-flavored stock, meat or shellfish, a thickener, and vegetables, is the official state cuisine of Louisiana. Its origins date back to the late 1800s, and many food historians believe the dish evolved from kingombo, an okra-based stew introduced to colonial Louisiana by enslaved Africans. MAINE: Lobster rolls Maine lobster roll with coleslaw and french fries on a waterfront harbor in Maine. jenlo8/Shutterstock Maine is famous for its lobster rolls, largely because lobster is one of Maine's most profitable exports. However, while the first lobster roll can be traced back to Connecticut, Maine-style lobster rolls often feature cold lobster meat rather than warm, dressed with mayonnaise and served in a toasted bun. MARYLAND: Crab cakes Crab cakes. Causeway/Shutterstock Crab cakes likely trace back to Native American cooking in the Chesapeake Bay region of the United States. However, the first official recipe for crab cakes appeared in a cookbook written by Crosby Gaige in the 1930s, under the name "Maryland Crab Cakes," Baltimore Magazine reported. MASSACHUSETTS: New England-style clam chowder Clam chowder in a bread bowl from Quincy Market in Boston, Massachusetts. J Rook/Shutterstock Clam chowder has roots all over the Northeast, but New England-style clam chowder is said to have been first served in Boston at Ye Olde Union Oyster House in 1836, Eater reported. MICHIGAN: Wet burritos A wet burrito. David Tonelson/Shutterstock Wet burritos, which come covered in red chile sauce and tons of cheese, are said to have been created at the Beltline Bar in Grand Rapids, Michigan, according to the restaurant's website , which has reportedly sold 6 million burritos and counting. MINNESOTA: Corn dogs Corn dogs. Igor Dutina/Shutterstock While some say corn dogs, then called "corny dogs," were introduced at the State Fair of Texas between 1938 and 1942, Pronto Pup vendors at the Minnesota State Fair claim to have invented the first breaded-and-fried hot dog in 1942, Eater reported. MISSISSIPPI: Mississippi mud pie Mississippi mud pie. excursionista.net/Shutterstock Eater reported that Mississippi mud pie, a dessert made with pudding, cake, biscuits, ice cream, whipped cream, marshmallows, and some kind of liqueur like Kahlua or amaretto, originated somewhere in the Vicksburg or Natchez area. MISSOURI: Barbecue Joe's Kansas City Barbecue. Chiquita L./Yelp Henry Perry is known as the "father of Kansas City barbecue" — he began selling slow-smoked meats wrapped in newspaper for 25 cents in the Garment District of Kansas City, across the Missouri border, in the early 1900s. He later opened Kansas City's first official barbecue restaurant in an old trolley barn. Perry loved barbecue so much that, on his death certificate, his occupation was listed as "barbecue man." MONTANA: Meat pie Meat pie. Slawomir Fajer/Shutterstock Although meat pies have roots in Europe, they're especially popular in Montana, where they're better known as pasties. The handheld pies became a staple in Butte thanks to the area's large population of Irish and Cornish miners, who could easily carry them to work underground. NEBRASKA: Reuben sandwiches Reuben sandwich. Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group/Getty Images The classic Reuben sandwich, made with corned beef, sauerkraut, Swiss cheese, and Thousand Island dressing, and served on rye bread, was supposedly invented by an Omaha, Nebraska, grocer in 1925, the Nebraska State Historical Society reported. NEVADA: Shrimp cocktail Shrimp cocktail. Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images Although the shrimp cocktail may not have been invented in Nevada or even the United States, Las Vegas residents have certainly claimed it as their own. The Golden Gate Hotel & Casino says that in 1959, it introduced Las Vegas to its famous, world-recognized 50-cent shrimp cocktail. Ever since, visitors have enjoyed partaking in the city's signature dish. NEW HAMPSHIRE: Pancakes with maple syrup Pancakes with maple syrup. Shawn Patrick Ouellette/Portland Press Herald/Getty Images While Vermont produces more maple syrup than any other state , New Hampshire is also known for its syrup production. True Granite State natives are known to douse their pancakes in 100% New Hampshire syrup. NEW JERSEY: Disco fries Disco fries. Cristina.A/Shutterstock Disco fries, which are french fries smothered in gravy, mozzarella, and other toppings, originate from the Garden State. Local legend has it that the late-night dish got its name from the hordes of people pouring into New Jersey diners after a long night of dancing, in search of the perfect snack. NEW MEXICO: Green chile cheeseburgers Green chile cheeseburger. Chris Curtis/Shutterstock Green chiles are the state's signature vegetable, so it comes as no surprise that New Mexico natives would want to add the ingredient to their burgers. NEW YORK: Pizza New York pizza. ChameleonsEye/Shutterstock New York is undeniably famous for its pizza, from cheap and cheerful $1 slices to more gourmet versions. New York City is also home to the nation's first pizzeria, Lombardi's, which opened in Little Italy in 1905. NORTH CAROLINA: Krispy Kreme donuts Krispy Kreme donuts. Rachel Askinasi/Insider Krispy Kreme began operating in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, on July 13, 1937. At the time, the owner Vernon Rudolph was only selling his donuts to local grocery stores. However, after people passing by the bakery asked about the heavenly scent, he cut a hole in an outside wall and began selling glazed donuts to people on the sidewalk. NORTH DAKOTA: Walleye Fried walleye. Cathy Scola/Getty Images North Dakota is famous for its walleye, and the state is known not only for selling the fried fish on its own but also in sandwiches. OHIO: Cincinnati-style chili Cincinnati-style chili. Brent Hofacker/Shutterstock What's Cooking America reported that Cincinnati prides itself on being the chili capital of the United States with more than 180 chili parlors. Thinner in consistency and commonly served over pasta, the dish is slightly different from traditional chili. Cincinnati-style chili is also often topped with chopped onions, shredded cheese, beans, and crushed oyster crackers. OKLAHOMA: Chicken-fried steak Chicken-fried steak. bhofack2/Getty Images Chicken-fried steak often comes served with mashed potatoes and gravy and is popular all over the South. However, one state loves the dish so much that it decided to make it official. In 1988, Oklahomans named chicken-fried steak one of their state meals, the Oklahoma Historical Society reported. OREGON: Clams Clams. Shutterstock Clamming is a popular activity in Oregon, where shellfish is abundant. So, it makes perfect sense that one of the most famous dishes from Oregon would involve clams. PENNSYLVANIA: Philly cheesesteak Philly cheesesteak. Shutterstock The state's most famous food by far is the classic Philly cheesesteak, which is believed to have been invented by a hot dog vendor in 1930, Visit Philadelphia reported. The sandwich contains thinly cut steak handsomely topped with cheese on a roll, plus sautéed onions, peppers, mushrooms, mayonnaise, hot sauce, salt, pepper, or ketchup. RHODE ISLAND: Stuffed clams Stuffed clams. ProArtWork/Getty Images Known locally as "stuffies" or stuffed quahogs, stuffed clams are considered Rhode Island's unofficial state dish. The classic recipe combines chopped clam meat with breadcrumbs, herbs, onion, bell pepper, and celery, then packs the mixture back into a clamshell and bakes it until golden. SOUTH CAROLINA: Shrimp and grits Shrimp and grits. Brent Hofacker/Shutterstock Although the exact origins of shrimp and grits are debated, many historians believe the dish originated in Charleston or elsewhere along the Carolina coast. Today, it's considered one of South Carolina's signature dishes and is a staple on menus across the state. SOUTH DAKOTA: Navajo tacos Navajo tacos. val lawless/Shutterstock Instead of traditional taco shells, those in South Dakota use frybread, which is flattened dough cooked in hot oil until puffy and crispy, to make Navajo tacos. However, while the dish is delicious, it also has a controversial history. Native Americans living in South Dakota invented the dish, but it was less about making a tasty meal and more about survival. Lisa Ironcloud, who works with food sovereignty programs, told Argus Leader that frybread was invented because Native Americans could make it using rationed ingredients like yeast and because it "filled their stomachs." TENNESSEE: Nashville hot chicken Nashville hot chicken. bhofack2/Shutterstock Nashville hot chicken, which is famous for being extremely spicy, also has quite a spicy history. Nashville hot chicken was invented when Thornton Prince, the owner of Prince's Hot Chicken, where legend says it was first created, came home to find his lover upset. To get revenge, she served him chicken covered in extra-hot spices. However, Prince liked the dish so much that he decided to open a restaurant and serve a version of it to local people in Nashville. TEXAS: Barbecue A person cooking barbecue. lazyllama/Shutterstock Texas is practically synonymous with barbecue. While every barbecue region has its own traditions, Texas-style barbecue stands apart for its emphasis on slow-smoked beef, particularly brisket, rather than pork. Seasoned simply with salt and pepper or a house rub and cooked low and slow over wood, Texas barbecue has become one of the state's defining culinary traditions and a draw for barbecue lovers from around the world. UTAH: Pastrami burgers Pastrami burgers. Tatty B./Yelp The New York Times reported that pastrami burgers were popularized by Crown Burgers in Salt Lake City, and are still one of the city's most famous foods. The burgers come topped with a Thousand Island-style sauce as well as tomatoes, shaved lettuce, and onions, but can also come served with cheese or other toppings. VERMONT: Vermont corn chowder Corn chowder. zepp1969/Getty Images Vermont corn chowder is a state-favorite dish made with a milk-based broth, corn, and other vegetables like onions, potatoes, and cabbage, thickened with flour or Vermont cheddar cheese. Bacon is also commonly added to the dish. VIRGINIA: Oysters A man shucking an oyster. ButtermilkgirlVirginia/Shutterstock Virginia's government website claims that "Virginia is for Oyster Lovers," and there's a reason. Not only is Virginia home to multiple oyster festivals but Virginia oysters can be harvested in eight different regions of the state. WASHINGTON: Fish and chips Fish and chips. Igor Sh/Shutterstock While fish and chips are often thought of as a quintessentially British dish , the state of Washington is equally famous for its flaky, fried fish and chips. WEST VIRGINIA: Biscuits and gravy Biscuits and gravy. Bonnie Jo Mount/The Washington Post/Getty Images The roots of biscuits and gravy can be traced back to the Southern Appalachian region of the United States in the late 1800s. The Washington Post reported that the earliest version of this Southern food used sausage gravy, which was also called "sawmill gravy" at the time. Historians believe that the food was hearty enough to power sawmill workers through their long days lifting heavy logs, and also thick and flavorful enough to make biscuits of that era "more palatable." WISCONSIN: Fried cheese curds Fried cheese curds. Paul Drinkwater/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal/Getty Images Fried cheese curds are a favorite dish in Wisconsin, the state famous for its cheese and dairy products. What's Cooking America reported that cheese factories in the state have to make cheese curds daily to meet the high demand for the product. WYOMING: Bison burgers The bison burger at Senator's Steakhouse & Brass Buffalo Saloon in Cheyenne, Wyoming. Autumn Parry/For The Washington Post via Getty Images Bison has long been associated with Wyoming, from the wild herds that have historically roamed the region to the private ranches that raise the animals across the state today. As such, the meat reflects Wyoming's Western and ranching identity. The state's tourism office says, when it comes to popular dishes, Wyoming is best known for bison, as well as elk, venison, and locally caught trout. Bison appears on menus across the state, including at Senator's Steakhouse & Brass Buffalo Saloon in Cheyenne (pictured). Read the original article on Business Insider

Some are also tied to major industries that support jobs, tourism, and local economies within their states, such as Alaska's salmon, Wisconsin's cheese, and Virginia's oysters.

Here's the most iconic local dish from every state.

ALABAMA: Chicken with white barbecue sauce
Chicken with white barbecue sauce.

Jacek Chabraszewski/Shutterstock

Alabama's famous white barbecue sauce, which is made with mayonnaise, vinegar, salt, and ground black pepper, is described as both creamy and tangy.

The sauce, which is said to have been invented in the 1920s by Bob Gibson of Big Bob Gibson Bar-B-Q in Decatur, Alabama, often comes served on a sandwich or with grilled or fried chicken.

ALASKA: Smoked salmon
Smoked salmon.

Frank Perry/AFP via Getty Images

Alaska is famous for its salmon, though locals may disagree on the best way to prepare it — whether that's smoked, grilled, or pan-seared.

For a classic Alaskan meal, serve the fish with seasonal vegetables, or enjoy smoked salmon on a bagel with cream cheese.

ARIZONA: Chimichangas
Chimichangas.

Ezume Images/Shutterstock

You might not know that chimichangas were invented in Arizona.

As Tucson Foodie reported, two restaurants in Tucson claim to have originated the dish, a large meat burrito filled with vegetables and spices, deep-fried, and topped with cheese and sauce.

ARKANSAS: Fried pickles
Fried pickles.

Kay Ecker/Shutterstock

Fans of fried pickles have Arkansas to thank for the iconic snack. The first fried dill pickles ever sold anywhere first appeared on the menu of the Duchess Drive-In in Atkins, Arkansas, in the summer of 1963, Encyclopedia of Arkansas reported.

CALIFORNIA: Avocado toast
Avocado toast.

Alexander Spatari/Getty Images

California is famous for its avocados, so it should come as no surprise that avocado toast is one of the most popular and famous local dishes in the Golden State. The San Francisco Chronicle reported that California residents have been making avocado toast for more than 130 years.

An issue of The Daily Alta California from 1885 lists a recipe that suggests spreading avocado "on slices of bread, and season with salt and pepper."

COLORADO: The "Fool's Gold" sandwich
"Fool's Gold" sandwiches.

Karl Gehring/The Denver Post/Getty Images

The now-closed Colorado Mine Company restaurant in Denver invented the original Fool's Gold sandwich: a hollowed-out loaf of sourdough stuffed with peanut butter, blueberry jam, and a pound of bacon.

The over-the-top sandwich became legendary after Elvis Presley reportedly loved it so much that he flew his private jet to Denver and back in a single night just to eat one.

CONNECTICUT: Warm lobster rolls
Lobster roll.

Rebecca Fondren Photo/Shutterstock

Culture Trip reported that the first documented lobster roll was served at a Milford, Connecticut, restaurant named Perry's in 1929.

Although you may be more familiar with Maine-style lobster rolls served cold with mayonnaise, Connecticut has its own signature take.

A traditional Connecticut-style lobster roll features warm lobster meat lightly dressed with melted butter and served on a split-top bun.

DELAWARE: Peach pie
Peach pie.

zoryanchik/Shutterstock

Delaware's official state dessert is peach pie, and peaches are an integral part of the state's agricultural industry.

According to the Delaware government, peaches have been an important part of the state's agricultural heritage since their introduction during Colonial times, when they became a major industry in the 19th century.

At the industry's peak in 1875, Delaware shipped about 6 million baskets of peaches to market.

FLORIDA: Cuban sandwiches
Cuban Sandwich.

Old Republic Kitchen and Bar/Yelp

While these sandwiches can, of course, be traced back to Cuba, what we know now as a "Cuban sandwich" is largely thanks to Cuban immigrants in Tampa, Florida.

Thrillist reported that the sandwiches made in Cuba and the United States had a few key differences when it came to ingredients.

The Florida version, which sometimes used imported Italian salami, became known as a "Cuban sandwich."

GEORGIA: Brunswick stew
Brunswick stew.

ButtermilkgirlVirginia/Shutterstock

Both Brunswick County, Virginia, and Brunswick, Georgia, claim to be the birthplace of Brunswick stew.

In Brunswick, Georgia, a town monument features a 25-gallon iron pot with an inscription stating that the first batch of Brunswick stew was cooked in it in 1898.

HAWAII: Kālua pork
Kalua pork nachos.

Maricay/Shutterstock

Kālua pork is one of Hawaii's most iconic dishes. The smoked, shredded pork — sometimes mixed with cabbage — is traditionally cooked in an underground oven, which is reflected in its name: "kālua" means "to cook in an underground oven" in Hawaiian.

IDAHO: Finger steaks
Finger steaks.

Paul_Brighton/Shutterstock

Many have traced the origin of finger steaks — fried pieces of beef — back to Milo's Torch Lounge in Boise.

Idaho Beef says chef Milo Bybee invented the dish in 1957 to use the restaurant's leftover tenderloin.

ILLINOIS: Deep-dish pizza
Giordano's.

Irene Jiang/Business Insider

While you might assume that all pizza originates in Italy, deep-dish pizza is actually American.

The BBC reported that restaurant owners Ike Sewell and Ric Riccardo introduced their creation, an Italian-American pizza they called deep-dish, at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago's Near North Side neighborhood in 1943.

INDIANA: Pork tenderloin sandwiches
A Hoosier sandwich.

Jeff R Clow/Getty Images

Pork tenderloin sandwiches, also called "Hoosier sandwiches," can be traced back to Nick Freienstein, a Huntington, Indiana, native-born to German parents. Eater reported the dish was originally inspired by Wiener schnitzel, a Viennese-style veal dish that is breaded and pan-fried.

In 1904, Freienstein began selling sandwiches and burgers out of a food cart. While veal was hard to come by in his hometown, pork was readily available. After he added pickles and onions to his fried pork tenderloin sandwich, Freienstein's cart took off. He is credited with creating the first "Hoosier sandwich."

IOWA: Fried catfish
Fried catfish and fries.

HMR2017/Shutterstock

While fried catfish is a popular dish throughout the South, Iowans are fond of it as well.

KANSAS: Loose meat sandwiches
Loose meat sandwiches.

P Lansing/Shutterstock

A cross between a sloppy Joe and a cheeseburger, loose meat sandwiches are a favorite among Kansas locals.

The Nu-Way Cafe, a Wichita-based chain of restaurants, is famous for its loose meat sandwiches. In other parts of the country, they are known as tavern sandwiches or Maid-Rites, named after the Iowa chain.

KENTUCKY: Beer cheese
Beer cheese.

Africa Studio/Shutterstock

According to local lore, beer cheese was invented by Chef Joe Allman for his cousin Johnnie, the owner of the Driftwood Inn near Winchester, Kentucky.

The Downtown Winchester Beer Cheese Festival reported that the dish was originally created by Allman to entice customers to order more beer with their meals.

LOUISIANA: Gumbo
Chicken and sausage gumbo.

Ken Durden/Shutterstock

Gumbo, a traditional stew consisting primarily of a strong-flavored stock, meat or shellfish, a thickener, and vegetables, is the official state cuisine of Louisiana.

Its origins date back to the late 1800s, and many food historians believe the dish evolved from kingombo, an okra-based stew introduced to colonial Louisiana by enslaved Africans.

MAINE: Lobster rolls
Maine lobster roll with coleslaw and french fries on a waterfront harbor in Maine.

jenlo8/Shutterstock

Maine is famous for its lobster rolls, largely because lobster is one of Maine's most profitable exports.

However, while the first lobster roll can be traced back to Connecticut, Maine-style lobster rolls often feature cold lobster meat rather than warm, dressed with mayonnaise and served in a toasted bun.

MARYLAND: Crab cakes
Crab cakes.

Causeway/Shutterstock

Crab cakes likely trace back to Native American cooking in the Chesapeake Bay region of the United States.

However, the first official recipe for crab cakes appeared in a cookbook written by Crosby Gaige in the 1930s, under the name "Maryland Crab Cakes," Baltimore Magazine reported.

MASSACHUSETTS: New England-style clam chowder
Clam chowder in a bread bowl from Quincy Market in Boston, Massachusetts.

J Rook/Shutterstock

Clam chowder has roots all over the Northeast, but New England-style clam chowder is said to have been first served in Boston at Ye Olde Union Oyster House in 1836, Eater reported.

MICHIGAN: Wet burritos
A wet burrito.

David Tonelson/Shutterstock

Wet burritos, which come covered in red chile sauce and tons of cheese, are said to have been created at the Beltline Bar in Grand Rapids, Michigan, according to the restaurant's website, which has reportedly sold 6 million burritos and counting.

MINNESOTA: Corn dogs
Corn dogs.

Igor Dutina/Shutterstock

While some say corn dogs, then called "corny dogs," were introduced at the State Fair of Texas between 1938 and 1942, Pronto Pup vendors at the Minnesota State Fair claim to have invented the first breaded-and-fried hot dog in 1942, Eater reported.

MISSISSIPPI: Mississippi mud pie
Mississippi mud pie.

excursionista.net/Shutterstock

Eater reported that Mississippi mud pie, a dessert made with pudding, cake, biscuits, ice cream, whipped cream, marshmallows, and some kind of liqueur like Kahlua or amaretto, originated somewhere in the Vicksburg or Natchez area.

MISSOURI: Barbecue
Joe's Kansas City Barbecue.

Chiquita L./Yelp

Henry Perry is known as the "father of Kansas City barbecue" — he began selling slow-smoked meats wrapped in newspaper for 25 cents in the Garment District of Kansas City, across the Missouri border, in the early 1900s.

He later opened Kansas City's first official barbecue restaurant in an old trolley barn. Perry loved barbecue so much that, on his death certificate, his occupation was listed as "barbecue man."

MONTANA: Meat pie
Meat pie.

Slawomir Fajer/Shutterstock

Although meat pies have roots in Europe, they're especially popular in Montana, where they're better known as pasties.

The handheld pies became a staple in Butte thanks to the area's large population of Irish and Cornish miners, who could easily carry them to work underground.

NEBRASKA: Reuben sandwiches
Reuben sandwich.

Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group/Getty Images

The classic Reuben sandwich, made with corned beef, sauerkraut, Swiss cheese, and Thousand Island dressing, and served on rye bread, was supposedly invented by an Omaha, Nebraska, grocer in 1925, the Nebraska State Historical Society reported. 

NEVADA: Shrimp cocktail
Shrimp cocktail.

Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images

Although the shrimp cocktail may not have been invented in Nevada or even the United States, Las Vegas residents have certainly claimed it as their own.

The Golden Gate Hotel & Casino says that in 1959, it introduced Las Vegas to its famous, world-recognized 50-cent shrimp cocktail. Ever since, visitors have enjoyed partaking in the city's signature dish.

NEW HAMPSHIRE: Pancakes with maple syrup
Pancakes with maple syrup.

Shawn Patrick Ouellette/Portland Press Herald/Getty Images

While Vermont produces more maple syrup than any other state, New Hampshire is also known for its syrup production. True Granite State natives are known to douse their pancakes in 100% New Hampshire syrup.

NEW JERSEY: Disco fries
Disco fries.

Cristina.A/Shutterstock

Disco fries, which are french fries smothered in gravy, mozzarella, and other toppings, originate from the Garden State.

Local legend has it that the late-night dish got its name from the hordes of people pouring into New Jersey diners after a long night of dancing, in search of the perfect snack.

NEW MEXICO: Green chile cheeseburgers
Green chile cheeseburger.

Chris Curtis/Shutterstock

Green chiles are the state's signature vegetable, so it comes as no surprise that New Mexico natives would want to add the ingredient to their burgers.

NEW YORK: Pizza
New York pizza.

ChameleonsEye/Shutterstock

New York is undeniably famous for its pizza, from cheap and cheerful $1 slices to more gourmet versions. New York City is also home to the nation's first pizzeria, Lombardi's, which opened in Little Italy in 1905. 

NORTH CAROLINA: Krispy Kreme donuts
Krispy Kreme donuts.

Rachel Askinasi/Insider

Krispy Kreme began operating in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, on July 13, 1937. At the time, the owner Vernon Rudolph was only selling his donuts to local grocery stores.

However, after people passing by the bakery asked about the heavenly scent, he cut a hole in an outside wall and began selling glazed donuts to people on the sidewalk.

NORTH DAKOTA: Walleye
Fried walleye.

Cathy Scola/Getty Images

North Dakota is famous for its walleye, and the state is known not only for selling the fried fish on its own but also in sandwiches.

OHIO: Cincinnati-style chili
Cincinnati-style chili.

Brent Hofacker/Shutterstock

What's Cooking America reported that Cincinnati prides itself on being the chili capital of the United States with more than 180 chili parlors. Thinner in consistency and commonly served over pasta, the dish is slightly different from traditional chili.

Cincinnati-style chili is also often topped with chopped onions, shredded cheese, beans, and crushed oyster crackers. 

OKLAHOMA: Chicken-fried steak
Chicken-fried steak.

bhofack2/Getty Images

Chicken-fried steak often comes served with mashed potatoes and gravy and is popular all over the South.

However, one state loves the dish so much that it decided to make it official. In 1988, Oklahomans named chicken-fried steak one of their state meals, the Oklahoma Historical Society reported.

OREGON: Clams
Clams.

Shutterstock

Clamming is a popular activity in Oregon, where shellfish is abundant. So, it makes perfect sense that one of the most famous dishes from Oregon would involve clams.

PENNSYLVANIA: Philly cheesesteak
Philly cheesesteak.

Shutterstock

The state's most famous food by far is the classic Philly cheesesteak, which is believed to have been invented by a hot dog vendor in 1930, Visit Philadelphia reported. 

The sandwich contains thinly cut steak handsomely topped with cheese on a roll, plus sautéed onions, peppers, mushrooms, mayonnaise, hot sauce, salt, pepper, or ketchup.

RHODE ISLAND: Stuffed clams
Stuffed clams.

ProArtWork/Getty Images

Known locally as "stuffies" or stuffed quahogs, stuffed clams are considered Rhode Island's unofficial state dish.

The classic recipe combines chopped clam meat with breadcrumbs, herbs, onion, bell pepper, and celery, then packs the mixture back into a clamshell and bakes it until golden.

SOUTH CAROLINA: Shrimp and grits
Shrimp and grits.

Brent Hofacker/Shutterstock

Although the exact origins of shrimp and grits are debated, many historians believe the dish originated in Charleston or elsewhere along the Carolina coast.

Today, it's considered one of South Carolina's signature dishes and is a staple on menus across the state.

SOUTH DAKOTA: Navajo tacos
Navajo tacos.

val lawless/Shutterstock

Instead of traditional taco shells, those in South Dakota use frybread, which is flattened dough cooked in hot oil until puffy and crispy, to make Navajo tacos.

However, while the dish is delicious, it also has a controversial history. Native Americans living in South Dakota invented the dish, but it was less about making a tasty meal and more about survival. 

Lisa Ironcloud, who works with food sovereignty programs, told Argus Leader that frybread was invented because Native Americans could make it using rationed ingredients like yeast and because it "filled their stomachs."

TENNESSEE: Nashville hot chicken
Nashville hot chicken.

bhofack2/Shutterstock

Nashville hot chicken, which is famous for being extremely spicy, also has quite a spicy history. Nashville hot chicken was invented when Thornton Prince, the owner of Prince's Hot Chicken, where legend says it was first created, came home to find his lover upset.

To get revenge, she served him chicken covered in extra-hot spices. However, Prince liked the dish so much that he decided to open a restaurant and serve a version of it to local people in Nashville.

TEXAS: Barbecue
A person cooking barbecue.

lazyllama/Shutterstock

Texas is practically synonymous with barbecue. While every barbecue region has its own traditions, Texas-style barbecue stands apart for its emphasis on slow-smoked beef, particularly brisket, rather than pork.

Seasoned simply with salt and pepper or a house rub and cooked low and slow over wood, Texas barbecue has become one of the state's defining culinary traditions and a draw for barbecue lovers from around the world.

UTAH: Pastrami burgers
Pastrami burgers.

Tatty B./Yelp

The New York Times reported that pastrami burgers were popularized by Crown Burgers in Salt Lake City, and are still one of the city's most famous foods. The burgers come topped with a Thousand Island-style sauce as well as tomatoes, shaved lettuce, and onions, but can also come served with cheese or other toppings.

VERMONT: Vermont corn chowder
Corn chowder.

zepp1969/Getty Images

Vermont corn chowder is a state-favorite dish made with a milk-based broth, corn, and other vegetables like onions, potatoes, and cabbage, thickened with flour or Vermont cheddar cheese. Bacon is also commonly added to the dish.

VIRGINIA: Oysters
A man shucking an oyster.

ButtermilkgirlVirginia/Shutterstock

Virginia's government website claims that "Virginia is for Oyster Lovers," and there's a reason. Not only is Virginia home to multiple oyster festivals but Virginia oysters can be harvested in eight different regions of the state.

WASHINGTON: Fish and chips
Fish and chips.

Igor Sh/Shutterstock

While fish and chips are often thought of as a quintessentially British dish, the state of Washington is equally famous for its flaky, fried fish and chips.

WEST VIRGINIA: Biscuits and gravy
Biscuits and gravy.

Bonnie Jo Mount/The Washington Post/Getty Images

The roots of biscuits and gravy can be traced back to the Southern Appalachian region of the United States in the late 1800s. The Washington Post reported that the earliest version of this Southern food used sausage gravy, which was also called "sawmill gravy" at the time.

Historians believe that the food was hearty enough to power sawmill workers through their long days lifting heavy logs, and also thick and flavorful enough to make biscuits of that era "more palatable."

WISCONSIN: Fried cheese curds
Fried cheese curds.

Paul Drinkwater/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal/Getty Images

Fried cheese curds are a favorite dish in Wisconsin, the state famous for its cheese and dairy products. What's Cooking America reported that cheese factories in the state have to make cheese curds daily to meet the high demand for the product.

WYOMING: Bison burgers
The bison burger at Senator's Steakhouse & Brass Buffalo Saloon in Cheyenne, Wyoming.

Autumn Parry/For The Washington Post via Getty Images

Bison has long been associated with Wyoming, from the wild herds that have historically roamed the region to the private ranches that raise the animals across the state today.

As such, the meat reflects Wyoming's Western and ranching identity. The state's tourism office says, when it comes to popular dishes, Wyoming is best known for bison, as well as elk, venison, and locally caught trout.

Bison appears on menus across the state, including at Senator's Steakhouse & Brass Buffalo Saloon in Cheyenne (pictured).

items.title: I learned poker to get ahead at work. I'm more empowered in my career and have made incredible connections.
items.summary: Playing poker every month has made me better at my job and helped me expand my network. Andrea Javor Every month, I play poker with a group of businesswomen to expand my professional network. The game has improved my decision-making under pressure and boosted my confidence as a leader. While counting chips and placing bets, I've also been able to connect with incredible professionals. Growing up, I didn't view poker as a game for girls. My dad and brothers constantly played, with the sounds of them placing their bets and shuffling cards always in my periphery. But I was never invited to join them. One time, they let me join a game of Texas Hold 'Em without fully explaining the rules, only to raise the bets early and push me out as quickly as possible. I was frustrated and vowed never to play at another unwelcoming table. Decades later, when I found out my new job offered a membership to a networking organization that was hosting an all-women poker night with limited seating, I eagerly signed up, even though I only knew the basics of the game. It felt like a community I wanted to be part of since childhood. Plus, I was curious about whether the game could help me level up my networking abilities. I needed an outlet to develop a competitive edge in the workplace I never expected a card game would help strengthen my business skills. Andrea Javor When I joined this initial poker night, I was at the midpoint of my advertising career. I'd spoken on a number of panels and was regularly meeting with a business coach to sharpen my leadership skills. But I still thought I needed to invest more in personal development, which, in turn, could help me at the office. My coach and I brainstormed innovative ways for me to maintain a competitive edge, but I never expected that playing a card game would help me hone enviable business skills. I'm already extremely extroverted, so schmoozing has never been a problem for me, but I still thought the poker night would be a great way to expand my reach of connections. Unfortunately, my poker prowess was limited to passively catching video clips over my boyfriend's shoulder. However, once I realized how heavily the game skewed male, I was determined to sharpen my skills. Plus, I wondered whether I'd pick up anything useful that could also help me in the corporate world . The night of the event, the room was alive with energy. The vibe was not at all intimidating, evidenced by wide smiles and warm energy. Every few minutes, a table erupted in cheers. The instructors made it easy to play, offering tips on how to think about probability and when to raise the pot. I won several hands while chatting with the other eight women at my table. When the event came to a close and the venue lights flipped on, no one wanted to leave. Someone shouted, "I've finally learned how to bet on myself, don't make us stop now!" I love that the game serves as a networking hub to empower others Every month, we spend hours playing and holding empowering conversations. Andrea Javor After that first poker night, a handful of us from the group committed to organizing a monthly game, and we've stuck together for over two years. I've felt the impact of regular attendance — it's improved my betting skills and helped me build long-term relationships. The table has also been a natural place to engage with peers, as we spend hours playing and chatting. Last month, I hosted 23 women from the group at my office, and the vibes were the antithesis of a smoky casino. I loved seeing the conference room set up with round tables, rather than the intimidating U-shaped seating it normally features. The room smelled like Jo Malone and popcorn. The playlist: Chappell Roan and Stevie Nicks. Our poker chips clicked like high heels on marble as I shuffled the deck with one hand and topped off my glass of pinot noir with the other. Being in the office this late was never more fun. As we moved the dealer button around the table, our conversation was intrinsically empowering. Someone mentioned they're interviewing for their next job, and another discussed their recent promotion — all while placing bets and counting chips. In my experience, poker skills beget business skills I love that this game has helped me feel more confident in my 9-to-5. Andrea Javor With all this poker experience under my belt, I've realized Texas Hold 'Em is analogous to the business I navigate every day. Senior advertising executives like me manage large teams and often make decisions under pressure with incomplete information. Poker trains me how to do just that, since I never know what cards my opponents are holding, but I have to check, bet, raise, or fold when it's my turn anyway. I've considered how the game helps each of us read a room — whether it's scanning for reactions when players look at their cards or reading faces in the boardroom, the skill is the same. Overall, this game has made me more confident in my 9-to-5, especially when I have to make unpopular leadership decisions that frankly don't always work out as expected. In poker, when I lose a hand, I don't cower away from betting on the next one. Each hand dealt is a fresh start, like a new day of the workweek. Additionally, this hobby has allowed me to meet incredible professionals and help them achieve big wins off the felt. I recently connected with a first-time player who was moving from London to Chicago. She was looking for contract positions, and I gladly introduced her to my human resources lead. We named our group "She Runs The Table," an antidote to belittling #GirlMath posts on TikTok, a manicured counterpoint to a culture that sometimes tells us to shrink our bets and smile as we fold. But at our table, we ante up and continually raise the stakes. Read the original article on Business Insider

The instructors made it easy to play, offering tips on how to think about probability and when to raise the pot.

I won several hands while chatting with the other eight women at my table.

When the event came to a close and the venue lights flipped on, no one wanted to leave. Someone shouted, "I've finally learned how to bet on myself, don't make us stop now!"

I love that the game serves as a networking hub to empower othersEvery month, we spend hours playing and holding empowering conversations.

Andrea Javor

After that first poker night, a handful of us from the group committed to organizing a monthly game, and we've stuck together for over two years.

I've felt the impact of regular attendance — it's improved my betting skills and helped me build long-term relationships. The table has also been a natural place to engage with peers, as we spend hours playing and chatting.

Last month, I hosted 23 women from the group at my office, and the vibes were the antithesis of a smoky casino.

I loved seeing the conference room set up with round tables, rather than the intimidating U-shaped seating it normally features.

The room smelled like Jo Malone and popcorn. The playlist: Chappell Roan and Stevie Nicks. Our poker chips clicked like high heels on marble as I shuffled the deck with one hand and topped off my glass of pinot noir with the other. Being in the office this late was never more fun.

As we moved the dealer button around the table, our conversation was intrinsically empowering.

Someone mentioned they're interviewing for their next job, and another discussed their recent promotion — all while placing bets and counting chips.

In my experience, poker skills beget business skillsI love that this game has helped me feel more confident in my 9-to-5.

Andrea Javor

With all this poker experience under my belt, I've realized Texas Hold 'Em is analogous to the business I navigate every day.

Senior advertising executives like me manage large teams and often make decisions under pressure with incomplete information. Poker trains me how to do just that, since I never know what cards my opponents are holding, but I have to check, bet, raise, or fold when it's my turn anyway.

I've considered how the game helps each of us read a room — whether it's scanning for reactions when players look at their cards or reading faces in the boardroom, the skill is the same.

Overall, this game has made me more confident in my 9-to-5, especially when I have to make unpopular leadership decisions that frankly don't always work out as expected.

In poker, when I lose a hand, I don't cower away from betting on the next one. Each hand dealt is a fresh start, like a new day of the workweek.

Additionally, this hobby has allowed me to meet incredible professionals and help them achieve big wins off the felt.

I recently connected with a first-time player who was moving from London to Chicago. She was looking for contract positions, and I gladly introduced her to my human resources lead.

We named our group "She Runs The Table," an antidote to belittling #GirlMath posts on TikTok, a manicured counterpoint to a culture that sometimes tells us to shrink our bets and smile as we fold.

But at our table, we ante up and continually raise the stakes.

items.title: I built two wholesale businesses. When I retired at 72, I volunteered to raise service dogs to keep myself on a routine.
items.summary: Jerry Burns says raising puppies gives his days structure after retirement. Courtesy of Jerry Burns Jerry Burns, 74, is a little more than a year into retirement. He started volunteering when he scaled back on work in his 60s. Raising a puppy has given his days structure and connected him to other volunteers. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jerry Burns, a puppy raiser with Guiding Eyes for the Blind . It has been edited for length and clarity. I ran my own businesses for 53 years. First, I did wholesale sales of tobacco and candy. When I sold my partnership stake after more than three decades, I decided to focus on candy and snacks, avoiding the negativity of tobacco. We expanded into novelty goods and nostalgia items, which turned out to be a very good decision: It was a more enjoyable workday, and the margins were bigger. I liked being an entrepreneur, but in my late 60s , I scaled back so I was only working about four hours a day. That's when I first started thinking about volunteer work. I knew I wanted a sense of purpose in the next phase of my life. I've always loved dogs , so I reached out to Guiding Eyes for the Blind, which has three puppy-raising facilities near me. I came for the dogs, but I stayed because the organization was so well-run. As a businessman, I appreciated that. I was drawn to the German Shepherds in the program I started volunteering regularly with Guiding Eyes for the Blind. I would help feed and walk dogs at the breeding kennel near my home. Often, I would bring a dog home with me in between my visits. Jerry Burns was drawn to German Shepherds. Courtesy of Jerry Burns While most dogs in the program are Labrador retrievers, about 10% are German Shepherds. The Shepherds are amazingly smart dogs, but they often struggle in the kennel — they can become overwhelmed and act out by barking or jumping. I had a German Shepherd in my 20s, and was immediately drawn to the breed again once I started volunteering. When I brought one home, the dog would immediately calm down and be able to fulfill its potential. I even hand-fed one dog, who was having a particularly difficult time with kennel life. I started fostering a breeding dog, then raising his puppy A little over a year ago, I sold my business and officially retired. I was fostering a shepherd who was a stud in the breeding program. That dog, Kohl, was supposed to be a long-term placement in my home, and I was thrilled at the idea. He was the perfect fit for my family. Then Guiding Eyes decided to place Kohl in more formal training. I was a bit sad, but I thought if that's the plan, that's what we have to do. Kohl was meant to go on to bigger and better things. Right around the same time, I was asked to become a puppy raiser for one of Kohl's puppies. It seemed like the perfect timing. I was used to getting up at 7 a.m. every day and being out the door by 8. If I had a puppy to train, I could continue that schedule. I wanted to have structure in retirement and not find myself wondering, "What am I going to do today?" I love the pup like my other dogs, but I know she's not mine That's how I ended up with Geneva. About a month after she came home, we got a call that Kohl, her father, was being removed from the training program. I was thrilled to adopt him and have him join my mini Australian shepherd as a pet. Over the past year, I've attended training with Geneva, and loved her like the other dogs in my house. Still, I know she's not mine to keep: this summer, she'll be moving on to formal service dog training. Puppy raisers typically have a dog for about 14-18 months. When I give her treats or pats, I remind her (and myself) that she's going to do great things. I've connected with a community through the program The visually impaired people who use service dogs have had a tremendous impact on me. Hearing their stories showed me what a home run this program is, and I'm so glad to be part of it, even in a small way. I've met great dogs through Guiding Eyes, but I've also met great people. I have a community of probably 25 puppy raisers, who go on walks and have dinner together to celebrate when a puppy is ready to move on to formal training. Oftentimes, the puppy raiser already knows they'll be getting another placement. I'm not sure my wife is ready for that, but Guiding Eyes has told me there will be another shepherd puppy ready for placement in the fall, soon after Geneva leaves. I might not be able to say no. items.summary_html:
Jerry Burns says raising puppies gives his days structure after retirement.

Courtesy of Jerry Burns

  • Jerry Burns, 74, is a little more than a year into retirement.
  • He started volunteering when he scaled back on work in his 60s.
  • Raising a puppy has given his days structure and connected him to other volunteers.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jerry Burns, a puppy raiser with Guiding Eyes for the Blind. It has been edited for length and clarity.

I ran my own businesses for 53 years. First, I did wholesale sales of tobacco and candy. When I sold my partnership stake after more than three decades, I decided to focus on candy and snacks, avoiding the negativity of tobacco. We expanded into novelty goods and nostalgia items, which turned out to be a very good decision: It was a more enjoyable workday, and the margins were bigger.

I liked being an entrepreneur, but in my late 60s, I scaled back so I was only working about four hours a day. That's when I first started thinking about volunteer work. I knew I wanted a sense of purpose in the next phase of my life.

I've always loved dogs, so I reached out to Guiding Eyes for the Blind, which has three puppy-raising facilities near me. I came for the dogs, but I stayed because the organization was so well-run. As a businessman, I appreciated that.

I was drawn to the German Shepherds in the program

I started volunteering regularly with Guiding Eyes for the Blind. I would help feed and walk dogs at the breeding kennel near my home. Often, I would bring a dog home with me in between my visits.

Jerry Burns was drawn to German Shepherds.

Courtesy of Jerry Burns

While most dogs in the program are Labrador retrievers, about 10% are German Shepherds. The Shepherds are amazingly smart dogs, but they often struggle in the kennel — they can become overwhelmed and act out by barking or jumping.

I had a German Shepherd in my 20s, and was immediately drawn to the breed again once I started volunteering. When I brought one home, the dog would immediately calm down and be able to fulfill its potential. I even hand-fed one dog, who was having a particularly difficult time with kennel life.

I started fostering a breeding dog, then raising his puppy

A little over a year ago, I sold my business and officially retired. I was fostering a shepherd who was a stud in the breeding program. That dog, Kohl, was supposed to be a long-term placement in my home, and I was thrilled at the idea. He was the perfect fit for my family.

Then Guiding Eyes decided to place Kohl in more formal training. I was a bit sad, but I thought if that's the plan, that's what we have to do. Kohl was meant to go on to bigger and better things.

Right around the same time, I was asked to become a puppy raiser for one of Kohl's puppies. It seemed like the perfect timing. I was used to getting up at 7 a.m. every day and being out the door by 8. If I had a puppy to train, I could continue that schedule. I wanted to have structure in retirement and not find myself wondering, "What am I going to do today?"

I love the pup like my other dogs, but I know she's not mine

That's how I ended up with Geneva. About a month after she came home, we got a call that Kohl, her father, was being removed from the training program. I was thrilled to adopt him and have him join my mini Australian shepherd as a pet.

Over the past year, I've attended training with Geneva, and loved her like the other dogs in my house. Still, I know she's not mine to keep: this summer, she'll be moving on to formal service dog training. Puppy raisers typically have a dog for about 14-18 months. When I give her treats or pats, I remind her (and myself) that she's going to do great things.

I've connected with a community through the program

The visually impaired people who use service dogs have had a tremendous impact on me. Hearing their stories showed me what a home run this program is, and I'm so glad to be part of it, even in a small way.

I've met great dogs through Guiding Eyes, but I've also met great people. I have a community of probably 25 puppy raisers, who go on walks and have dinner together to celebrate when a puppy is ready to move on to formal training.

Oftentimes, the puppy raiser already knows they'll be getting another placement. I'm not sure my wife is ready for that, but Guiding Eyes has told me there will be another shepherd puppy ready for placement in the fall, soon after Geneva leaves. I might not be able to say no.

items.title: What We Actually Know About China’s AI Export Controls
items.summary: Since June 2026, Chinese officials have been in closed door talks about restricting foreign access to the country’s most advanced AI models, both open and closed. The Ministry of Commerce is leading the discussions, China’s state planning agency is also in the mix, and the companies involved include Alibaba, ByteDance, and Zhipu. Nothing has been decided. There is no published regulation, only reported meetings and one unofficial proposal from a legal scholar roundtable, and the options range from light registration for basic tools to keeping the most capable future models domestic only. ( enlarge ) My practical read is not that Chinese open models are about to disappear. It is that I would stop assuming every future release from Alibaba, Zhipu, or DeepSeek will keep showing up globally, immediately, with downloadable weights. If your product depends on a Chinese open model, it is worth keeping a backup provider in your back pocket and avoiding a build that only works with one model family. The earliest real signal will probably come from how the major Chinese labs actually ship their next models, not from a dramatic overnight ban.
